title: Regularization: Ridge and Lasso
description: Penalized least squares, shrinkage, sparsity, and the Bayesian meaning of the penalty.
overview: Least squares has two weak points. When features are numerous or nearly collinear, the estimate is unstable: small changes in the data produce large changes in θ̂. And a flexible model fits noise. Both problems are cured by the same step: add a penalty on the size of the parameters, trading a little bias for a large reduction in variance.

This chapter develops the two standard penalties. Ridge shrinks all coefficients smoothly. Lasso sets many exactly to zero and so performs feature selection. We derive their solutions, picture them geometrically, and show that each is a maximum a posteriori estimate under a prior on the weights.
objectives: Write the ridge and lasso objectives and solve ridge in closed form.
Explain ridge shrinkage through the SVD and compute effective degrees of freedom.
Explain geometrically why L1 gives sparse solutions and L2 does not, and compute soft thresholding.
Interpret each penalty as a prior and relate λ to the noise and prior variances.
Choose the regularization strength by validation, and prepare features correctly.

sections.title: Ridge regression
body: Why would large weights be a problem? A model that overfits typically needs enormous weights: to bend a curve through every noisy point it uses large positive and negative terms that nearly cancel. For example, fitting 10 points with a degree-9 polynomial can produce weights in the thousands, while the underlying trend needs weights near 1. So a simple remedy is to make large weights expensive. Fitting the data still lowers the cost, but every unit of weight size raises it, and the optimizer must find a compromise. That is what a penalty does.
**Ridge regression** adds the squared L2 norm of the weights (the sum of their squares, ‖θ‖² = θ₁² + θ₂² + …) to the least squares objective:

The **regularization strength** λ sets the tradeoff. At λ = 0 the objective is ordinary least squares. As λ grows, the weights are pulled toward zero. The intercept θ₀ is normally left out of the penalty, because shifting all labels by a constant should not change the slopes; center y and the features, or exclude θ₀ in the code.
The gradient is 2Xᵀ(Xθ − y) + 2λθ. Setting it to zero gives the closed form

body.key: XᵀX is positive semidefinite, so XᵀX + λI has eigenvalues at least λ > 0 and is always invertible. Ridge solves the singularity problem: it works with more features than examples and with collinear features.

body.h: What ridge does: the SVD view

body: In plain terms: the data determine some combinations of the features very well and others hardly at all. Ridge leaves the well-determined combinations almost alone and shrinks the poorly determined ones hard, because those are where noise would otherwise be mistaken for signal. The formulas below say this exactly.
Write X = UΣVᵀ with singular values σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ …. The least squares fit is Xθ̂ = Σ_j u_j (u_jᵀy). The ridge fit is

Each component of y along a principal direction u_j is shrunk by the factor σ_j²/(σ_j² + λ). Directions with large singular values (well determined by the data) are barely touched, and directions with small singular values (where the data say little and noise dominates) are shrunk heavily. The sum of the shrinkage factors is the **effective degrees of freedom**,

body.eq: df(λ) = Σ_j σ_j²/(σ_j² + λ),    from n + 1 at λ = 0 down to 0 as λ → ∞

example.title: Shrinkage in one dimension
example.problem: Fit y = θx with no intercept to x = (1, 2, 3), y = (2, 3, 5). Find the least squares and ridge solutions for λ = 7. Then find the effective degrees of freedom of a model whose squared singular values are 10, 1 and 0.1, for λ = 1.
solution: The ridge weight is the least squares weight times 14/21 = 2/3.
With squared singular values 10, 1, 0.1 and λ = 1, the factors are 10/11 = 0.909, 1/2 = 0.5 and 0.1/1.1 = 0.091, so df = 1.5. The effective model has 1.5 degrees of freedom instead of 3.

body: Ridge is biased: E[θ̂_ridge] = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹XᵀXθ, which is shorter than θ. Its variance is smaller, and for some λ > 0 its total mean squared error is lower than that of least squares (a theorem of Hoerl and Kennard). The shrinkage example in the Generalization chapter shows the mechanism in the simplest setting.

check.q: Why is XᵀX + λI invertible for any λ > 0?
check.a: Its eigenvalues are all at least λ, so none is zero
wrong: XᵀX has full rank for any data
Adding λI makes the matrix diagonal
λI cancels the zero eigenvalues of XᵀX exactly

sections.title: The lasso and sparsity
body: The **lasso** (least absolute shrinkage and selection operator) penalizes the L1 norm:

body.eq: J_lasso(θ) = ½‖Xθ − y‖² + λ‖θ‖₁ = ½‖Xθ − y‖² + λ Σ_j |θ_j|

body: Think of the penalty as a budget. The total absolute size of all weights, |θ₁| + |θ₂| + …, may not exceed some amount. With a tight budget, spending on a weak feature is not worth it: the weight is more valuable on a strong feature, so the weak feature gets exactly zero. Ridge, whose cost is squared, behaves differently: the cost of a tiny weight is negligible, so it keeps every feature a little.

The L1 penalty has a corner at zero, so the lasso sets many coefficients //exactly// to zero. The solution is **sparse**, which makes the model interpretable and performs **feature selection** automatically. There is no closed form in general, but the problem is convex and is solved by **coordinate descent** (update one coefficient at a time with the others fixed) or proximal gradient methods.

An equivalent view minimizes the squared error subject to a bound on the penalty, ‖θ‖ ≤ t. The error contours are ellipses centered at the least squares solution. The solution is the first point where an ellipse touches the constraint region. The L2 ball is round, and the touching point is generic, with all coordinates non-zero. The L1 ball is a diamond with vertices on the axes, and an ellipse usually meets it first at a vertex, where some coordinates are zero. In high dimensions the L1 ball has even more corners and edges.

example.title: Ridge versus lasso on orthonormal features
example.problem: The least squares coefficients are z = (3.0, −0.4, 1.2). Apply ridge and lasso with λ = 0.5 (and X orthonormal).
solution: Ridge shrinks every coefficient proportionally and keeps the small one. The lasso subtracts a fixed amount, which removes the small coefficient altogether and shrinks the large one by only 0.5.

list: **Elastic net** uses λ₁‖θ‖₁ + λ₂‖θ‖₂². It keeps the lasso's sparsity but, unlike the lasso, tends to select or drop groups of correlated features together instead of picking one arbitrarily.
The lasso selects at most m features when n > m.
The **group lasso** penalizes the norms of groups of coefficients, so a whole group (such as all dummy variables for one category) enters or leaves together.
The **L0 penalty**, the count of non-zero weights, gives true subset selection, but the problem is combinatorial.

check.why: Soft thresholding gives (0.9, 0, −0.4). Only the entry with |z| ≤ 0.5 is zeroed.

sections.title: Regularization as a prior
body: The penalty has a second reading that explains where it comes from. Before seeing any data you probably believe that most weights are small, and that huge weights are unlikely. A **prior** writes that belief down as a probability distribution over the weights. The data then pull the estimate toward the values that fit, and the prior pulls it toward the values you thought likely beforehand. The compromise is the penalized solution.

Formally, treat θ as a random vector with a **prior** distribution p(θ) that expresses beliefs before seeing data. Bayes' rule gives the posterior p(θ | data) ∝ p(data | θ) p(θ). The **maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimate maximizes the posterior, which is the same as maximizing log-likelihood plus log-prior:

body.eq: θ̂_MAP = argmax_θ [ log p(y | X, θ) + log p(θ) ]

body: With Gaussian noise of variance σ², the log-likelihood is −‖y − Xθ‖²/(2σ²) up to a constant. Now consider two priors.

list: **Gaussian prior** θ_j ~ N(0, τ²): log p(θ) = −‖θ‖²/(2τ²) + const. Multiplying the objective by 2σ² gives ridge with **λ = σ²/τ²**.
**Laplace prior** p(θ_j) ∝ exp(−|θ_j|/b): log p(θ) = −‖θ‖₁/b + const. The MAP estimate is the lasso: multiplying the negative log posterior by σ² gives ½‖y − Xθ‖² + λ‖θ‖₁ with λ = σ²/b.

example.title: Reading λ from the prior
example.problem: Labels have noise variance σ² = 1, and we believe each weight is roughly within ±0.5 of zero (standard deviation τ = 0.5). What ridge λ corresponds?
example.solution: λ = σ²/τ² = 1/0.25 = 4. A tighter prior (smaller τ) gives a larger λ and stronger shrinkage; more noise also gives a larger λ, because the data deserve less trust relative to the prior.

body: As the data set grows, the likelihood term (a sum over m examples) dominates the fixed prior term, and the MAP estimate approaches the maximum likelihood estimate. The same objective in neural network training is called **weight decay**, and it is implemented by shrinking the weights a little at every update. The Bayesian Methods chapter treats the full posterior instead of only its peak.

sections.title: Choosing and using the penalty
body: The strength λ is a hyperparameter, so choose it by validation.

list: Fit the model over a grid of λ values spaced geometrically (for example 10⁻⁴ to 10²), and evaluate each by cross-validation. The plot of the coefficients against λ is the **regularization path**: coefficients shrink toward zero as λ increases, and for the lasso they hit zero one by one.
Pick the λ with the lowest validation error, or the largest λ within one standard error of the best (the 'one-standard-error rule'), which gives a simpler model of nearly equal quality.
At λ = 0 the training error is smallest. As λ grows, training error rises monotonically, while validation error traces the usual U shape.

body.warn: The penalty depends on the scale of each feature. A feature measured in meters needs a coefficient 1000 times larger than the same feature in millimeters, and so is penalized differently. Standardize all features (using training-set statistics) before applying ridge or lasso, and do not penalize the intercept.

body.tip: Use the lasso when you believe only a few features matter or need an interpretable short list. Use ridge when many features each carry a little signal. Use the elastic net when features are correlated and you also want sparsity.

body: Penalties on the weights appear throughout machine learning: the soft-margin parameter C of a support vector machine plays the role of 1/λ, weight decay is applied to neural networks, and trees are regularized by limiting depth. The shared principle is that restricting a model's effective complexity reduces variance, and the amount of restriction is tuned on held-out data.

check.q: Why standardize features before ridge or lasso?
check.a: The penalty treats all weights equally, so it depends on feature scale
wrong: The intercept would otherwise be penalized
Standardization changes the number of features

summary: Ridge minimizes ‖Xθ − y‖² + λ‖θ‖². The solution (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy always exists and shrinks each singular direction by σ²/(σ² + λ).
The lasso minimizes ½‖Xθ − y‖² + λ‖θ‖₁. It sets coefficients exactly to zero because the L1 ball has corners on the axes. With orthonormal features it is soft thresholding.
Ridge is the MAP estimate under a Gaussian prior with λ = σ²/τ², and the lasso under a Laplace prior.
Penalties trade bias for variance. Choose λ by cross-validation on a log grid, standardize the features, and do not penalize the intercept.
The elastic net combines both penalties and is useful with correlated features.

problems.q: Ridge with λ = 3 is fit to a one-feature model with XᵀX = 12 and Xᵀy = 30. Find the least squares and ridge slopes and the shrinkage factor.
problems.solution: θ̂_ols = 30/12 = 2.5. θ̂_ridge = 30/(12 + 3) = 2. The shrinkage factor is 12/15 = 0.8.

problems.q: Squared singular values of X are 16, 4 and 1. Compute the effective degrees of freedom of ridge for λ = 4.
OLS coefficients on orthonormal features are (−2.2, 0.9, 0.2, 1.6). Find the lasso solution for λ = 1.
Show that with more features than examples (n > m) the matrix XᵀX is singular but XᵀX + λI is not.
problems.solution: rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) ≤ m < n, and XᵀX is n×n, so it has a zero eigenvalue. XᵀX is positive semidefinite, so all its eigenvalues are ≥ 0, and those of XᵀX + λI are ≥ λ > 0. A matrix with no zero eigenvalue is invertible.
problems.a: XᵀX has a zero eigenvalue. Adding λI moves every eigenvalue up by λ.

problems.q: A lasso path shows a coefficient that becomes non-zero only when λ falls below 0.8. Another becomes non-zero below 0.3. Which feature does the model consider more important, and why?
problems.solution: The first. The lasso retains a feature only if its gradient correlation with the residual exceeds λ. A feature that enters at the larger λ has the stronger association with the response, given the features already chosen.
